details:
What it does and how it works

Sal a la vista (“Salt in sight”) is a web app that helps irrigated farmers in San Juan, Argentina, spot fields that are degrading before it is too late. In our study area (25 de Mayo and surroundings), 24,332 ha were cultivated over the last 11 seasons, and about one in four hectares (5,963 ha) stopped producing. Salt is one of the known causes: it arrives with irrigation water and rising groundwater, and by the time the white crust appears on the surface the field is already lost.

We downloaded and processed 11 seasons (2015/16 to 2025/26) of NASA data, lot by lot:

  • HLS v2.0 (Harmonized Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2, 30 m): greenness, shortwave and thermal signals, the bare-soil calendar and the risk map.
  • GIBS natural-color HLS imagery: lot photos and a 10-year diagnosis of every field.
  • ECOSTRESS (evaporative stress index and land surface temperature, 70 m): plant stress.
  • NASA POWER (monthly rain and maximum temperature): 3-month salinization pressure and climate context.

A logistic regression learns from 2015/16 to 2019/20 which lots stopped producing in 2023/24 to 2025/26. It is trained on one half of the area and tested on the other, both ways. In the riskiest 20% of lots, 55 out of 100 actually stopped producing, compared with 31 picked at random. Applying the same lag to recent seasons, the app forecasts which lots are most at risk around 2029/30 to 2031/32.

A farmer marks a lot on the map and gets a card with what happened to it in 10 years, its risk and the forecast. On bare lots it shows a first, preliminary salt signal and indicates where to measure. It then compares three 3-season crop rotations according to what the farmer prioritizes: saving water, recovering the soil or keeping sales. It works on a computer and on a phone, in the field.

Benefits and expected impact

Farmers and extension agents get an early warning years before the damage is visible, plus a concrete next step: where to measure salt and which rotation to try. This helps them protect their income, use scarce irrigation water better and keep productive land in a desert region that lives on irrigation. Each field confirmation from a farmer becomes ground truth to improve the salt model. The approach can be extended to other irrigated oases, such as the Tulum Valley.

Tools and technologies

Data processing in Python (numpy, scipy, pandas, rasterio, pyproj) and Node.js. The web app is built with Vite, React and MapLibre GL, with Esri World Imagery as the basemap, and is deployed on Vercel. NASA data: HLS v2.0 (LP DAAC), GIBS, ECOSTRESS (JPL) and POWER (LaRC). Other sources: measured soil conductivity from Guida-Johnson et al. (2026) to train the salt model, INTA soil profiles (SISINTA) to test it, and FAO and USDA references for crop water needs, rooting depth and salt tolerance.

What makes it creative

The satellite cannot see salt under a crop. Instead of pretending it can, we combine what it does see (a field losing greenness, the soil changing color, plant stress) with ten years of history to rank fields by risk. We then close the loop in the field: the app asks the farmer to confirm what they see and to enter a soil measurement. It turns open NASA data into a lot-level decision tool in the farmer’s own language.

Factors our team considered

  • Honesty about limits. The risk is a ranking between lots, not a probability. The salt estimate is preliminary and relative, with no dS/m: against 18 INTA profiles it reached a correlation of 0.52 (p = 0.056). The app labels every result as validated, indicator or estimate, and always asks for field confirmation.
  • Validation against reality. We used a spatial train/test split and checked the model against what actually happened, not only against itself.
  • Usability for farmers. Plain language, three simple steps, Spanish and English, and a mobile version for use in the field.
  • Local context. Data from San Juan farms and INTA. Rotations are based on general FAO and USDA references that should be validated with INTA San Juan.
  • Open and traceable. Every source and method is listed in the app, and the code is published on GitHub.
